title: Central Otago
description: The world's southernmost major wine region: mountains, schist and vivid Pinot Noir.
L: Central Otago lies in the south of New Zealand's South Island, around 45 degrees south, near Queenstown. It's the world's southernmost major wine region. Vineyards sit in valleys and on slopes between mountains, at about 200 to 450 m, on schist, gravel and loess. Sub-regions include Gibbston, Bannockburn, Cromwell Basin, Bendigo and Wanaka.

Unlike the rest of New Zealand, Central Otago has a continental climate, far from the sea and sheltered by mountains: hot, dry summer days, cold nights, cold winters and low rainfall, about 350 mm a year in some areas. Frost is a major risk in spring and autumn; growers use wind machines and helicopters. Irrigation is common.
What makes Central Otago's climate unusual for New Zealand?
It's continental, far from the sea
Mountains and distance from the coast make it continental.

In the 1860s, a gold rush brought miners to Central Otago, and a French miner, Jean Désiré Féraud, planted vines around 1864. The industry faded. Modern winemaking began in the 1980s, with pioneers like Rolfe and Lois Mills at Rippon, on Lake Wanaka, and Alan Brady at Gibbston Valley. Bannockburn's old gold sluicings now sit among vineyards.
Central Otago has a maritime climate.
Not true. It's New Zealand's only continental wine region.

Explain why it suits the region

Pinot Noir covers about 80% of Central Otago's vineyards. Its style is vivid: deep for Pinot, with dark cherry, plum, raspberry, thyme and spice, fresh acidity and silky tannins. Intense sunshine and UV light give colour and ripe fruit; cold nights keep acidity. Sub-regions differ: Bannockburn is warm and rich, Gibbston cooler and more delicate.

Pinot Gris, Riesling and Chardonnay are the main whites, with high acidity and purity. Some producers make traditional method sparkling wine from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Wild thyme, which grows on the hillsides, is often noted in the wines' aromas.
Match each sub-region to its feature.
Each Central Otago sub-region has its style.
Wild thyme grows across Central Otago's hills, and many tasters find a herbal, thyme note in its Pinot Noir.
Why is Central Otago Pinot Noir so deeply coloured for Pinot?
Strong light thickens skins and deepens colour.

Reading Central Otago and eating with it

Labels show the grape, Central Otago GI and often a sub-region, like Bannockburn or Gibbston. New Zealand's 85% rules apply, and screw caps are standard. Many producers are small and family-owned; some make single-vineyard wines.

Central Otago Pinot Noir suits lamb, especially New Zealand lamb, venison, duck, salmon and mushrooms. Its herbal, thyme notes suit herb-crusted meat. Pinot Gris and Riesling suit seafood and Asian food. Serve Pinot at 14 to 16 degrees; good examples age 8 to 12 years.
Which dish suits Central Otago Pinot Noir?
Its fruit and thyme notes suit herbed lamb.
Queenstown, the nearby adventure-sports capital, makes Central Otago one of New Zealand's most visited wine regions.
Central Otago Pinot Noir suits venison.
Yes. Its fruit and acidity suit lean game.
